title: Climate change and international security
summary: Should the Security Council treat climate change as a threat to peace? Envoys, reports, mission mandates, early warning and sovereignty split the permanent members.

committee.name: Security Council: climate change and security (practice)
committee.notes: A practice draft written for class; not an adopted UN text. Council membership as the platform knows it for 2026; check before use. Positions are estimates from the linked UN records.

topic.name: Climate change as a threat to international peace and security
topic.notes: Real topic. Positions are estimates from the linked UN records; countries without a position are treated as unknown.

tags.council_forum: Keeps climate change and security on the Security Council's own agenda
tags.sg_reports: Asks the Secretary-General for regular reports on climate-related security risks
tags.mission_mandates: Requires peacekeeping and political missions to assess climate risk
tags.special_envoy: Appoints a UN Special Envoy on climate and security
tags.early_warning: Builds early-warning systems and shared climate data to prevent conflict
tags.host_consent: Limits climate-risk work in a country to what its government agrees to
tags.climate_finance: Links the Council's work to climate finance for vulnerable countries

resolution.title: Climate change and the maintenance of international peace and security

preambular.text: Recalling the Charter of the United Nations and the primary responsibility of the Security Council for the maintenance of international peace and security,
Recalling the Paris Agreement and the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change,
Noting that droughts, floods, rising seas and food shortages affect communities in many parts of the world,
Reaffirming that Member States shall settle their disputes by peaceful means,

operative.text: Decides to keep climate change and its effects on peace and security as a regular item on the agenda of the Council;
Requests the Secretary-General to report to the Council every year on climate-related risks to peace and security in the situations on its agenda;
Decides that peacekeeping operations and special political missions shall assess climate-related risks and include them in their planning and reports;
Requests the Secretary-General to appoint a Special Envoy on climate and security, who will advise the Council and brief it twice a year;
Encourages the United Nations to build early-warning systems and share climate data openly, so that tensions can be spotted before they turn violent;
Decides that any assessment of climate-related security risks in a country shall be carried out only with the consent of its government;
Calls upon developed countries to keep their climate finance promises to the countries most exposed to climate risks, including those affected by conflict.

cards.text: Requests the Secretary-General to include climate-related security risks in the existing reports on each country, rather than in a separate report;
Requests the Secretary-General to appoint a Special Envoy on climate and security, who will work only with the consent of the countries concerned;
Encourages peacekeeping operations to include climate advisers where the host government agrees;
Decides that the mandates of all peacekeeping operations shall include an assessment of climate-related security risks;
Calls upon regional organisations to share early-warning information on drought, floods and food insecurity with the United Nations;
Decides to hold an open debate on climate change and security once a year;
Encourages States in a position to do so to support climate adaptation in fragile and conflict-affected countries;
Requests that climate early-warning data be shared with host governments first, respecting their decisions on how it is used;

events.title: A permanent member sets out its red line
events.body: One permanent member tells colleagues it cannot accept any climate work in a country without that government's agreement.
events.teaches: Because of the veto, each permanent member's red lines shape every Security Council text.

events.title: Elected members speak together
events.body: The ten elected members agree a joint statement asking the Council to keep climate risks on its agenda.
events.teaches: Elected members serve two-year terms and often coordinate to increase their influence on the Council.

events.title: Small island States address the Council
events.body: Small island developing States ask to speak in an open debate and describe what rising seas mean for their security.
events.teaches: Countries that aren't members can be invited to speak at the Council under its rules of procedure.

events.title: A scientist briefs Council members
events.body: A climate scientist explains to Council members how early warnings could reduce the risk of disputes over water and food.
events.teaches: The Council often hears expert briefers, including in informal Arria-formula meetings.

events.title: Closed consultations run late
events.body: Council members spend the afternoon in closed consultations, leaving little time for meetings with other delegations.
events.teaches: Much Security Council negotiation happens in closed consultations, away from the public chamber.

events.title: A co-sponsor wavers over host consent
events.body: A co-sponsor of the draft hesitates over the host consent wording and asks you to help find language it can defend at home.
events.teaches: Drafters keep a coalition together by finding wording each co-sponsor can defend to its government.

author: Claude Sonnet (delegated), 4 Nov 2026; to be checked by B. Gough
